paragraphs: This paper investigates what repeated self-attention does to the representations of tokens. Its central tool is a decomposition of a network’s output into paths: each path follows a sequence of attention heads through successive layers. This makes it possible to analyze smaller contributions to the output and then understand their combined effect.

The analysis reveals a strong tendency toward token uniformity. In a network without skip connections or multilayer perceptrons, the output approaches a rank-one matrix doubly exponentially with depth. In plain language, the representations increasingly lose the distinctions that allow different tokens to carry different information. The result concerns this pure-attention setting, making the architectural conditions essential to interpreting the claim.

The authors also show that skip connections and multilayer perceptrons prevent this degeneration, and experiments on standard transformer architectures verify the convergence findings. The contribution therefore explains why these components matter alongside attention: they help preserve representational distinctions that repeatedly applying attention alone tends to erase.
icml-2021-attention-is-not-all-you-need-.tldr: Pure self-attention rapidly drives token representations toward rank one, while skip connections and multilayer perceptrons prevent this degeneration.

paragraphs: Bilinear Classes provide a shared framework for studying when reinforcement learning can generalize through function approximation. Instead of treating each tractable model separately, the paper identifies a structural class encompassing nearly all existing models with polynomial sample complexity. It also includes new cases, notably one where both optimal action values and optimal state values are linear in known features.

The main result supplies an algorithm with polynomial sample complexity for this class. Its guarantee is expressed through the generalization error of an underlying supervised learning problem. This connection matters because it relates the amount of interaction needed for reinforcement learning to the statistical difficulty of a learning subproblem. For existing models, the resulting bounds nearly match the best previously known guarantees.

The framework also reaches infinite-dimensional kernel feature spaces. For the specified linear value-function and transition models, the bounds depend on information-theoretic quantities rather than explicitly on feature dimension. This allows the analysis to remain meaningful even when the feature representation itself is infinite-dimensional.
icml-2021-bilinear-classes-a-structural-.tldr: Bilinear Classes unify many provably learnable reinforcement learning models and connect their sample requirements to supervised generalization.

paragraphs: Prediction services distribute work across machines, but a slow worker or failed node can leave a requested prediction unavailable. Coded-InvNet addresses this problem by designing backup computation that helps recover missing results. Its starting point is a coded computation algorithm for invertible functions, connecting the mathematical structure of a prediction function to the resilience of the serving system.

The approach draws on invertible neural networks, Manifold Mixup, and domain translation methods. These ingredients connect machine learning design with the system’s ability to tolerate missing work. The central idea is that the form of the model and the design of its backup tasks can be considered together when building a resilient prediction service.

Experiments show that Coded-InvNet can outperform existing approaches, especially with compute overhead as low as 10%. In the reported example, a backup task recovers a missing prediction with 85.9% accuracy without knowing which of ten workers will fail. The abstract reports a 32.5% improvement over the previous state of the art, demonstrating useful recovery under a small resource allowance.
icml-2021-coded-invnet-for-resilient-pre.tldr: Coded-InvNet combines invertible-model ideas with backup computation to recover missing predictions under low compute overhead.

paragraphs: Learning systems often cannot ask for feedback after every action. This paper formalizes that restriction as a hard budget on reward queries, potentially changing over time. It studies the resulting decision problem in multi-armed bandits, linear contextual bandits, and reinforcement learning, where an agent must decide both what to do and when feedback is worth requesting.

A natural strategy is to query whenever the budget permits. The authors show that this greedy approach performs surprisingly well in fully stochastic settings. With adversity, however, it can incur linear regret, meaning accumulated decision losses can grow proportionally with the length of interaction. This makes the timing of feedback requests consequential when conditions are less favorable.

Confidence-Budget Matching instead requests feedback when a confidence interval is wider than the inverse square root of the available budget. The rule relates current uncertainty to the resources available for resolving it. Analyses across the studied settings show good performance even when adversity affects contexts, initial states, or budgets, supporting selective querying as a way to manage restricted feedback.
icml-2021-confidence-budget-matching-for.tldr: Confidence-Budget Matching uses uncertainty and available budget to decide when to request reward feedback.

paragraphs: Recovering a subspace from corrupted data requires identifying shared structure despite observations that do not belong to it. Earlier Dual Principal Component Pursuit methods largely focused on finding one direction perpendicular to a hyperplane containing the inliers. Extending that procedure by finding perpendicular directions sequentially is computationally expensive and lacks convergence guarantees.

This paper instead estimates an entire basis for the orthogonal complement simultaneously. It formulates that task as a nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization problem on the Grassmannian, a space whose elements represent subspaces. The holistic formulation treats the perpendicular directions as one geometric object, allowing the analysis to address recovery of the full subspace directly.

Geometric and statistical analyses establish global optimality results and show tolerance for outlier counts scaling as the square of the inlier count in the analyzed noiseless and noisy settings. A Riemannian regularity condition then supports linear convergence of a subgradient method to a neighborhood of the desired orthogonal subspace. The remaining error is proportional to the noise level, explicitly linking recovery precision to data corruption.
icml-2021-dual-principal-component-pursu.tldr: A holistic DPCP formulation estimates the full orthogonal subspace with robustness guarantees and linear convergence to noise-dependent accuracy.

paragraphs: EfficientMORL addresses the cost of learning object-centered representations without supervision. Existing approaches can require long training times and substantial memory, or give up useful structural biases. The paper focuses on retaining symmetry and disentanglement while reducing dependence on the expensive iterative inference used to handle their associated optimization challenges.

Inference proceeds in two stages. A hierarchical variational autoencoder first builds symmetric and disentangled representations through bottom-up processing. A lightweight network then refines those representations using top-down feedback. During training, a curriculum gradually reduces the number of refinement steps, encouraging the first stage to produce representations that need progressively less correction.

On the standard multi-object benchmark, the method demonstrates strong object decomposition and disentanglement while making training and test-time inference nearly an order of magnitude faster than the previous state-of-the-art model. With no refinement steps at test time, it retains 99.1% of refined decomposition performance. This finding supports using costly refinement as a training aid while substantially reducing the inference work ultimately needed.
icml-2021-efficient-iterative-amortized-.tldr: EfficientMORL learns object representations with progressively less iterative refinement, retaining most refined performance while substantially accelerating computation.

paragraphs: Evaluating strategies in a multi-agent setting often requires measuring how they perform against many other strategies. Methods such as alpha-rank can consequently demand an expensive collection of pairwise comparisons. This paper studies how to obtain a satisfactory ranking in two-player meta-games from only a subset of the payoff matrix.

The approach uses the observation that agents with similar skills may produce similar payoffs against opponents. Such shared behavior motivates low-rank matrix completion: reconstructing missing payoffs from a smaller observed set by exploiting structure in the matrix. The authors develop separate algorithms for exact payoff observations and for observations corrupted by noise.

For both settings, the theoretical analysis gives a requirement of O(nr log n) payoff entries for sufficiently good strategy evaluation, where n counts agents and r is the payoff matrix rank. Experiments on three synthetic and twelve real-world games show evaluation from a few entries can be comparable to methods given the entire matrix. The findings connect reduced evaluation cost to exploitable payoff structure rather than requiring exhaustive comparisons.
icml-2021-estimating-rank-from-a-few-ent.tldr: Low-rank payoff matrix completion enables alpha-rank-style strategy evaluation from a limited set of exact or noisy comparisons.

paragraphs: Persistence diagrams summarize topological structure in objects such as graphs, time series, and point clouds. When those objects are random, a statistical summary of their diagrams can be useful. Constructing something like an average is challenging because persistence diagrams do not inhabit an ordinary linear space where averaging coordinates automatically gives the desired summary.

The paper studies the Expected Persistence Diagram, represented as a measure on the plane, and estimates it with an empirical counterpart. The authors prove that this estimator achieves a parametric convergence rate and is minimax optimal over a large class of models. This establishes a statistical guarantee for a summary that is also simple and efficient to compute.

The empirical measure can nevertheless place mass at too many locations for convenient practical use. To address that issue, the paper develops a quantization algorithm that produces a measure supported on a smaller set. Its output approximates a quantization of the theoretical expected diagram at near-optimal rates, connecting a compact representation to a principled population-level target.
icml-2021-estimation-and-quantization-of.tldr: The paper establishes optimal estimation guarantees for expected persistence diagrams and near-optimal guarantees for compact quantized summaries.

paragraphs: Learning a graphical model usually starts with independent observations from its probability distribution. That assumption can be difficult to satisfy when observations come from a Markov chain that takes a long time to mix. This paper instead studies reconstruction of binary graphical models using correlated observations generated by a dynamical process, a setting natural to many applications.

The authors analyze the number of samples needed by two estimators. One uses an interaction screening objective, and the other uses a conditional likelihood loss. Both are examined in the dynamical-data setting, making the process that produces observations part of the learning analysis rather than treating every observation as an independent draw.

The reported finding is that samples from dynamics far from equilibrium can yield an exponential reduction in sample complexity compared with a quickly mixing dynamical process. This highlights the informational role of the observation process: data gathered away from equilibrium can be particularly useful for reconstruction in the studied setting. It motivates evaluating dynamics as a source of learning information, alongside the graphical model being recovered.
icml-2021-exponential-reduction-in-sampl.tldr: The studied estimators can reconstruct binary graphical models with exponentially fewer samples from far-from-equilibrium dynamics than from quickly mixing dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic Bregman gradient methods for minimizing relatively smooth convex functions. The analysis centers on how randomness in the gradients affects the final optimization accuracy. In particular, it relates convergence to the size of the gradient noise at the optimum, making that local quantity central to understanding what the basic method can achieve.

The authors prove that Bregman Stochastic Gradient Descent converges to a region whose size depends on this noise. When the noise is zero, as in the interpolation setting where the data is fitted perfectly, the method quickly reaches the exact minimizer. The distinction separates convergence to a noise-dependent neighborhood from convergence all the way to an optimum.

For objectives written as finite sums, the paper shows how variance reduction can counter nonzero noise. Fast convergence to the exact minimizer then follows under additional regularity assumptions on the Bregman reference function. Applications to Poisson-noise tomography and statistical preconditioning for distributed optimization illustrate the approach, connecting the theory to problems where relative smoothness is useful.
icml-2021-fast-stochastic-bregman-gradie.tldr: The analysis ties Bregman SGD accuracy to gradient noise and shows when variance reduction enables fast convergence to the exact optimum.

paragraphs: This paper uses convex optimization to examine the structure hidden inside a neural network training problem. It considers multiple three-layer ReLU subnetworks trained with weight decay. The authors show that this training problem has an equivalent convex formulation in a higher-dimensional space, providing another way to understand both its optimization and its regularization.

In the convex formulation, regularization takes the form of a group l1 penalty that promotes sparsity across groups. This reveals a feature-selection interpretation of the networks: the equivalent problem selects among high-dimensional features while controlling their complexity. The equivalence makes the regularizing effect of weight decay visible through a different mathematical representation.

The authors further prove that a standard convex solver can globally optimize the equivalent problem in time polynomial in sample count and data dimension when network width is fixed. That fixed-width condition is part of the computational guarantee. Experiments using synthetic and real datasets numerically validate the theoretical results, supporting this convex perspective on the specified three-layer training setup.
icml-2021-global-optimality-beyond-two-l.tldr: Training the studied three-layer ReLU subnetworks is equivalent to convex group-sparse feature selection, with polynomial-time global optimization at fixed width.

paragraphs: Kernel ridge regression has strong statistical guarantees in low dimensions, but those guarantees do not automatically explain its behavior in high-dimensional problems. This paper examines a shared property of many common kernels: rotational invariance. The examples covered include radial basis function kernels, inner-product kernels, and fully connected neural tangent kernels of any depth.

The authors establish a lower bound on generalization error across a wide range of data distributions and kernels with different eigenvalue decay patterns. In the high-dimensional settings studied, rotational invariance leads to inconsistent estimation unless the target is a low-degree polynomial. Being such a polynomial is an exception to this obstruction, rather than a universal guarantee of successful estimation.

The result changes what a useful high-dimensional analysis must examine. Eigenvalue decay alone does not capture the kernel structure responsible for the identified failure. The paper therefore argues that consistency analyses generally need a more detailed account of kernel structure. Its contribution is to expose a structural barrier that can persist despite spectral descriptions that appear favorable.
icml-2021-how-rotational-invariance-of-c.tldr: Rotational invariance creates a high-dimensional consistency barrier for common kernels unless the target is a low-degree polynomial.

paragraphs: Contrastive divergence is widely used to train energy-based models, but unstable training can limit its usefulness. This paper revisits a gradient term that is often omitted because it is difficult to calculate. The authors investigate whether that convenience discards information that materially affects the learning process and propose a training adaptation based on their findings.

They show that the term has a numerically significant contribution, can be estimated tractably, and matters in practice for avoiding instability. This gives a concrete reason to retain it in training rather than treating it as negligible. The paper also examines data augmentation and processing at multiple scales as ways to improve model robustness and generated outputs.

Empirical evaluation considers the stability of different model architectures and reports improved performance across image generation, out-of-distribution detection, and compositional generation. These results support the practical value of the revised training approach across several uses of energy-based models. The contribution combines a closer examination of the training gradient with complementary choices that improve robustness and generation quality.
icml-2021-improved-contrastive-divergenc.tldr: Estimating an often-omitted gradient term improves contrastive divergence training stability, with empirical gains across several energy-based modeling tasks.

paragraphs: Kernel-UCBVI addresses exploration and exploitation in finite-horizon reinforcement learning when states and actions come with a notion of distance. The method uses smoothness in the environment to share information across nearby state-action pairs. This supports learning in spaces where treating every possible pair as unrelated would discard useful structure.

The algorithm builds nonparametric kernel estimates of rewards and transitions, then uses an optimistic planning approach to guide decisions. The authors provide a regret bound of order H³K^(2d/(2d+1)), up to logarithmic factors, for K episodes of horizon H. Here d is the covering dimension of the joint state-action space, linking the guarantee to the space’s geometric complexity.

The paper presents this as the first regret guarantee for kernel-based reinforcement learning with smoothing kernels, under very weak assumptions on the decision process. Experiments in continuous environments with sparse rewards empirically validate the approach. Together, the analysis and experiments connect distance-based generalization with a finite-time account of how exploration costs accumulate during learning.
icml-2021-kernel-based-reinforcement-lea.tldr: Kernel-UCBVI combines kernel estimates and optimistic planning with a regret guarantee governed by state-action space geometry.

paragraphs: This paper examines network architecture as a component of adversarial training. Much attention has gone to training objectives and optimizers while retaining architectures developed for standard training. The authors argue that architecture and adversarial training should be considered together, because an architecture suited to standard training need not remain optimal under adversarial training.

Searching a large architecture space directly is costly because adversarial training is already time-consuming. The proposed diverse-structured network reduces that search space by using a small collection of predefined building blocks, such as residual blocks. This replaces decisions over many low-level operations with decisions over familiar, larger architectural components.

Within a searched block, DS-Net assigns weights to all of these atomic blocks instead of selecting just one. The design balances access to diverse structures with emphasis on useful ones, while keeping the architectural choices manageable. Empirical results demonstrate advantages of this weighting approach. The contribution is therefore a practical way to incorporate architectural adaptation into adversarial training without relying on a broad search over individual operations.
icml-2021-learning-diverse-structured-ne.tldr: DS-Net makes architecture adaptation for adversarial training more manageable by weighting a small set of predefined network blocks.

paragraphs: Energy-based models describe a distribution through a learned energy function and its associated Gibbs measure. Neural networks make that function expressive while providing a way to incorporate structure in the data. This paper focuses on shallow, overparameterized networks and asks how their training regime affects the statistical quality of the resulting generative model.

The authors compare an active training regime with its associated lazy, or kernel, regime. They show a statistical advantage for active training, specifically improved adaptation to hidden low-dimensional structure in the data distribution. This extends a type of advantage already observed in supervised learning to the energy-based generative modeling setting.

The analysis covers both maximum likelihood estimation and estimation based on Stein discrepancy. Numerical experiments on synthetic data validate the theoretical findings. The central implication is that the way a shallow network is trained matters alongside its capacity: active training can better exploit underlying low-dimensional organization than the corresponding kernel regime in the settings analyzed. The work connects overparameterization theory to the statistical behavior of generative models.
icml-2021-on-energy-based-models-with-ov.tldr: Actively trained shallow neural energy models adapt better to hidden low-dimensional structure than their associated lazy or kernel models.

paragraphs: Fully non-autoregressive translation faces a multimodality problem: alternative word arrangements complicate learning from a target sentence. This paper introduces order-agnostic cross entropy to reduce the effect of word reordering on training. The objective changes how predicted tokens are matched to reference tokens before the model receives its loss.

Instead of penalizing word-order errors directly, OaXE computes cross entropy under the best available alignment between predictions and target tokens. This lets the training objective focus on token agreement without requiring the original positional correspondence. Because logarithmic loss is sensitive to invalid references, the method also uses cross-entropy initialization and loss truncation to guide learning toward a useful portion of the search space.

Experiments on major WMT benchmarks report substantial translation improvements and a new state of the art for fully non-autoregressive models. Additional analyses find fewer repeated tokens and greater prediction confidence, supporting the claim that the objective alleviates multimodality. The results show how changing the alignment used by a training loss can improve this translation setting.
icml-2021-order-agnostic-cross-entropy-f.tldr: OaXE trains non-autoregressive translation using the best token alignment, reducing reordering penalties and improving translation performance.

paragraphs: Building symmetry into a model is widely expected to improve generalization, but precisely quantifying that benefit is difficult. This paper studies the question in linear models. It considers targets whose distributions are invariant or equivariant with respect to a compact group, placing the relationship between the target’s symmetry and the model’s structure at the center of the analysis.

Under this setting, the authors prove a strictly nonzero generalization improvement for invariant or equivariant models. The result supplies a concrete theoretical benefit rather than merely suggesting that symmetry might be useful. The analysis also reveals relationships among generalization, the number of training examples, and properties of the group action.

The proof builds on how averaging operators structure function spaces, with further consequences for feature averaging. This connects a mathematical operation used to express symmetry with its statistical effect on learning. The findings establish a precise advantage in the linear setting when the target has the relevant symmetry, and identify group structure and sample count as ingredients in understanding that advantage.
icml-2021-provably-strict-generalisation.tldr: For linear models with appropriately symmetric targets, the paper proves a strictly positive generalization benefit from invariance or equivariance.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use predictions to improve an underlying algorithm, raising the question of what the predictor should optimize. This paper studies that question for frequency estimation with a learned count-min sketch. A predictor identifies heavy hitters in a data stream, and those keys are counted explicitly outside the sketch.

The authors identify coverage as an approximately sufficient statistic for the remaining sketch’s performance. Coverage measures the normalized frequency mass of the keys selected for explicit counting. This links prediction quality to how much of the stream is handled outside the sketch, giving a training target tied directly to the downstream algorithm.

Models trained to optimize coverage produce large improvements over prior approaches in average absolute frequency error. The finding illustrates why a learning component should be designed around the system it supports: identifying keys matters through their contribution to the sketch’s eventual estimation accuracy. The paper turns that relationship into both a statistical characterization and an effective training objective for the predictor.
icml-2021-putting-the-learning-into-lear.tldr: Training heavy-hitter predictors to maximize covered frequency mass substantially improves learned count-min sketch frequency estimation.

paragraphs: Training an agent to follow one ethical theory assumes a level of moral agreement that people often do not share. This paper instead considers moral uncertainty: an agent assigns credence to several plausible ethical theories and takes that uncertainty into account when acting. It translates this philosophical idea into a reinforcement learning setting.

The authors propose two training methods that make different tradeoffs among competing desiderata, then train agents in simple environments. These experiments illustrate how uncertainty across theories can help restrain extreme behavior associated with commitment to a single theory. The findings concern these demonstrations rather than establishing ethical competence for autonomous deployment.

The work also exposes technical difficulties in representing moral disagreement through reinforcement learning. One central issue is how to make a principled tradeoff between reward functions that compete but lack a common basis for comparison. By making such problems computationally explicit, the paper both advances methods for acting under moral uncertainty and uses reinforcement learning to investigate questions from moral philosophy.
icml-2021-reinforcement-learning-under-m.tldr: Two reinforcement learning methods explore acting under moral uncertainty, illustrating reduced extremes and difficulties in comparing competing ethical rewards.

paragraphs: This paper uses convex analysis to characterize optimal hidden-layer weights in norm-regularized deep networks. It shows that a set of optimal weights can be identified as extreme points of a convex set. This gives a geometric description of network structure at an optimum and provides a common framework for examining several architectures and data settings.

For deep linear networks, the authors prove that optimal weight matrices align with preceding layers. They establish the same alignment for deep ReLU networks when the data is whitened. Another consequence is that norm-regularized deep ReLU networks perform spline interpolation on one-dimensional datasets, extending a characterization previously known for two-layer networks.

The framework also yields closed-form optimal weights for rank-one or whitened data. With batch normalization, the analysis applies to arbitrary data as well. The authors use these results to explain Neural Collapse, in which class means take the form of the vertices of a simplex equiangular tight frame. Together, the findings connect regularization and architectural structure to precise geometric properties of optimal representations.
icml-2021-revealing-the-structure-of-dee.tldr: Convex duality characterizes optimal deep-network weights, yielding alignment, spline, and Neural Collapse results under the specified settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies generalization in batch reinforcement learning with general value-function approximators. It treats Bellman error as a surrogate objective for the gap from optimal performance and asks when that error can be reliably estimated or minimized. Rademacher complexity supplies the measure of function-class richness used to express statistical guarantees.

The analysis separates two sampling regimes. With double sampling, the excess risk of empirical risk minimization is bounded by the function class’s Rademacher complexity. With single sampling, sample-efficient risk minimization is impossible without additional assumptions, regardless of the algorithm. Under completeness assumptions, however, analogous complexity bounds become available for fitted Q-iteration and a minimax-style algorithm.

The authors further use local Rademacher complexity to obtain fast statistical rates. Their results cover finite classes, linear spaces, kernel spaces, and sparse linear features. The contribution links familiar statistical learning tools to batch reinforcement learning while showing that the sampling regime and completeness assumptions materially affect what can be learned. Function-class complexity alone is therefore only part of the required statistical picture.
icml-2021-risk-bounds-and-rademacher-com.tldr: Rademacher complexity yields batch reinforcement learning risk bounds, with guarantees depending critically on sampling and completeness assumptions.

paragraphs: Hierarchical topic models discover document representations and topic taxonomies at multiple levels. However, common priors treat topics within a layer as independently drawn, overlooking relationships within and across layers. This paper introduces a gamma belief network guided by topic embeddings to capture those dependencies and the semantic similarities among topics.

Words and topics are represented by vectors with the same dimension. At each layer, the topic matrix is factorized into a factor loading matrix and a topic embedding matrix. The transpose of the embedding matrix becomes the factor loading matrix for the next layer. Repeating this sharing pattern creates the sawtooth factorization and directly links neighboring levels of the topic hierarchy.

An autoencoding variational inference network learns the model parameters through stochastic gradient descent. Experiments on large text corpora report better extraction of deeper interpretable topics and better document representations than other neural topic models. The contribution makes relationships among hierarchical topics part of the model’s parameterization, with empirical benefits for both interpreting the hierarchy and representing documents.
icml-2021-sawtooth-factorial-topic-embed.tldr: Shared word and topic embeddings connect adjacent layers of a gamma belief network, improving hierarchical topics and document representations.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can solve one environment yet struggle with unseen variations of the same problem. Self-Paced Context Evaluation addresses this by choosing a curriculum of problem instances during training. The aim is to use training interactions more efficiently while improving the policy’s ability to handle new tasks from the same domain.

SPaCE builds its curriculum online using information already contained in state-value estimates. This lets training progress inform which instances the agent encounters, with little additional computational overhead. The approach is independent of the particular problem domain and can be added to any reinforcement learning agent that approximates a state-value function.

Experiments with different value-based agents in two environments demonstrate faster learning and improved generalization. The reported acceleration reaches up to tenfold compared with the evaluated approaches, including round-robin selection and SPDRL. These findings support using the agent’s own value information to organize its training experiences. The claimed generalization concerns new variations within the same problem domain, matching the curriculum’s intended role.
icml-2021-self-paced-context-evaluation-.tldr: SPaCE uses state-value estimates to build training curricula, improving same-domain generalization and achieving up to tenfold faster learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Generating structured objects requires learning patterns in data while respecting rules that define valid outputs. XOR-Contrastive Divergence addresses both requirements within a single learning approach. It uses XOR-Sampling to obtain samples from the model distribution during contrastive divergence training, and the resulting method guarantees that generated structures satisfy the constraints.

For exponential-family models, the authors establish a linear convergence rate toward the global maximum of the likelihood function, up to a vanishing constant. This gives the approach a formal optimization guarantee in the stated model family. Constraint satisfaction also improves learning performance, connecting validity of generated structures with the model’s ability to learn from its training data.

Experiments cover data-driven experimental design, dispatching route generation, and sequence-based protein homology detection. Across these applications, the authors report superior performance over the tested baselines in generating valid structures and capturing the training set’s inductive bias. The contribution combines guaranteed validity, a qualified global convergence result, and empirical evidence that explicitly enforcing constraints can support effective learning.
icml-2021-xor-cd-linearly-convergent-con.tldr: XOR-CD guarantees valid constrained structures and provides linear convergence toward globally optimal likelihood, up to a vanishing constant, for exponential-family models.
